question: A 72-year-old man presents at 08:30 with sudden left-sided weakness onset at 08:10. He is hypertensive. Haemorrhage must be excluded before any treatment decision. Which imaging investigation should be performed FIRST?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI-DWI is more sensitive for early ischaemia but takes longer, is not always immediately available, and cannot be performed in patients with contraindications (pacemakers, agitation). NCCT is the first-line acute investigation.

Correct. NCCT brain is the mandatory first investigation in acute stroke: it is fast, universally available, and reliably detects haemorrhage (hyperdense) within minutes. Thrombolysis cannot be given until haemorrhage is excluded.
CTA is essential later in the workup (to assess for large vessel occlusion if thrombectomy is considered) but is NEVER the first investigation. Haemorrhage must be excluded by NCCT first.
Carotid Doppler is part of the aetiological workup for TIA/minor stroke to detect significant stenosis, but has no role in the emergency acute imaging decision.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Neuroimaging in Acute Stroke block. The rule: NCCT always first in the emergency setting to exclude haemorrhage — only then can you consider thrombolysis or further vascular imaging.
Good. Remember the sequence: NCCT first (exclude haemorrhage) → CTA/MRA (if thrombectomy candidate) → MRI-DWI (if diagnosis uncertain after NCCT). Speed matters: door-to-CT should be < 25 minutes.
